This is game 19 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k for game 19 and play Black. I’ll review the recent games, count area early, and check liberties and eye boundaries during fights, then save the full record and lessons.

# Game 18: White vs 20k — B+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Resigned after Black move 67 (J2). All 67 moves were stone moves.
Final captures: Black 12, White 4. No pass, invalid move or returned ko marker occurred.
No numerical final score or official dead-stone adjudication occurred.

The 20k series record is now four wins, nine losses and one draw. Retain 20k. The left survived, but the eleven-stone upper group was captured and the late lower-right attempt lacked two eyes.

## Records

- game-018.sgf contains all 67 moves and RE[B+R].
- game-018-log.json contains opponent selection, every play response, resignation, all 34 distinct returned playing positions with group/liberty inventories, the complete move list, provisional counts, and explicit corrections.
- All choices and variations were manual. Code only parsed current boards, counted present groups/liberties, recorded responses and converted moves to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.
- The independent secure left count was 16 White stones plus A2/B1 = 18 area. A8 was contested, not included in this guaranteed count. This is a local count, not a final-board score.

## Opening: early top footholds, but lower development narrowed

1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D3, 4 W C4, 5 B D4,
6 W C7, 7 B D5, 8 W E7, 9 B C5,
10 W C2, 11 B D2, 12 W G7, 13 B B4,
14 W B3, 15 B F6, 16 W C1, 17 B D1.

Unlike game 10, Black D4 joined D3 rather than allowing White D4/E3 to cut. White placed C7/E7/G7 early, but the lower group became a narrow left strip. C2/B3/C1 maintained connections without establishing enough eye space.

After move 9 the explicitly unsecured outline was lower A–C rows1–4 (12) plus A/B5 (2), upper A–E rows7–9 (15) plus A–C6 (3), total32. No life or secure territory was claimed.

After move13, the target was lower A–C rows1–3 plus C4 (10), upper A–G rows7–9 (21), A–C6 (3) and A/B5 (2), total36. B4 had already reduced the earlier outline. Every region still required boundary turns; G7 was only a foothold.

18 W A3, 19 B A2, 20 W A4, 21 B B5,
22 W A5, 23 B A6.

A4 ataried B4 at B5, but Black B5 connected to C5. A5 added the real orthogonal liberty A6; Black immediately occupied it. The eight White stones A3/A4/A5/B3/C1/C2/C3/C4 then had only B1/B2. This was a closed strip, not life.

Manual proof on that board: W B1, B B2 captures nine; W B2, B B1 captures nine. W A1, B B2, W B1 captures Black A2/B2 into the connected two-point A2/B2 space, but B A2 occupies the vital point; W B2 captures A2, then B A2 captures eleven. No seki or unconditional life. This diagnosis was valid for move23 and had to be rebuilt after the later capture.

Reconsider before B4/D1/A6 close the routes. Earlier lower expansion, a different response to D4, or different top/lower timing remain hypotheses; no single winning replacement was verified.

## A capture reopened the lower escape

24 W B6 put isolated Black A6 in atari at A7.
25 B B1 ignored it and left the lower White group only B2.
26 W A7 captured A6.
27 B C6, 28 W A6, 29 B B8,
30 W B7, 31 B D7, 32 W C8, 33 B D8.

The capture reopened A6 as a liberty for the previously trapped lower group, B6 and A7. W A6 then joined all three directly. B7 joined that group to C7. Capturing A6 and playing A6 were separate required actions.

The rescue depended on Black ignoring A6's atari with B1. It was not a forced life pattern. The initial intention was to abandon the lower stones and expand above; the returned inventory revealed that the capture had changed the lower group's status.

Black B8/D7/D8/C9 subsequently closed the upper escape. White used the remaining time to finish the lower eyes:

34 W B2, 35 B C9, 36 W A1 captured Black A2/B1,
37 B E8.

Before A1, Black A2 and B1 each had only A1, while the main White group retained A8. Black A1 would have been suicide because it captured neither White group. W A1 captured both Black stones.

Correction: A1 did NOT connect directly to B2. Its orthogonal neighbors A2/B1 were now empty; B2 is diagonal. The isolated A1 group and fifteen-stone main group each retained both separate A2/B1 eyes. A2 boundaries A1/A3/B2 and B1 boundaries A1/B2/C1 were White. Black at either eye captures neither group because both retain the other eye, so either fill is suicide.

This is the same-color disconnected shared-eye proof seen in game11, not the opposing-color shared-liberty trap. NEVER fill A2 or B1 to connect A1: the resulting joined group would lose an eye. Sixteen stones plus two eyes secured eighteen area.

## Upper development made only one eye

38 W F7, 39 B E6, 40 W G6, 41 B G5,
42 W H5, 43 B H6, 44 W H7, 45 B F8,
46 W J6 captured H6, 47 B H4,
48 W J5, 49 B J4, 50 W J7, 51 B H8,
52 W G8, 53 B G9.

F7 joined E7/G7. H5 contested the right boundary while broad lower space still existed, but H6 cut it from G6. H7 connected to G7 and ataried H6 at J6; Black F8 ignored this atari. J6 captured H6 and reopened H6 for all adjacent White groups.

J5 joined H5/J6, then J7 joined them to the upper group without filling H6. H6 had connected White G6/H5/H7/J6 boundaries. It was a single eye, not unconditional life.

The provisional upper-right count initially included Black F6 by mistake: F–J rows6–9 (16), E7 (1), F–J row5 (4), total21, plus left18 =39. This was corrected before G6: excluding already-Black F6 gives20, combined38. Even that outline assumed unprotected upper/row5 boundaries; G5/F8/H8/G9 promptly reduced it. None of the twenty upper-right points had been secured.

The important strategic warning came before the final threat: after Black F8 the upper group had only G8/H8/J7 routes; after H8/G9, the ten connected White stones had exactly H6/J8. The top lacked a second eye. Earlier G8/G9 or different boundary timing are unverified hypotheses, not established saves.

## Critical error: J8 filled the last outside liberty

54 W H9 double-ataried Black H8 at J8 and G9 at F9.
55 B J9 captured H9.
56 W J8, 57 B H6 captured ELEVEN White stones.

The new J8 stone's neighbors were H8 Black, J9 Black and J7 White. It added NO liberty. The connected eleven-stone White group now had exactly H6.

The in-game reading discussed B H9 joining the threatened Black groups, followed by W F9 capturing four, or B F9 followed by W H9 capturing two. These conditional branches did not prove a rescue: Black could ignore BOTH ataris and capture the entire White boundary group first at H6.

After B H6, all eleven captured points reopened liberties for H8/J9/G9 and neighboring Black groups. H8 and J9 were no longer in atari. This is the central tactical error of game18. The recorded optimistic rescue language is explicitly withdrawn.

H6 was geometrically an eye while White retained outside liberties, but one eye does not prevent capture on the last liberty. Before any proposed threat, compute your resulting group's actual liberties, then check whether the opponent can capture it immediately instead of answering. The current-board inventory was correct; the manual reading failed to use it.

Black captured twelve total: H9 plus E7/F7/G6/G7/G8/H5/H7/J5/J6/J7/J8.

## Late lower-right attempt failed its second-eye boundaries

58 W G2, 59 B G3, 60 W F2, 61 B F3,
62 W E2, 63 B E3, 64 W H2, 65 B H3,
66 W F1, 67 B J2. White resigned.

The entry had F2/G1/G3/H2 available, and named G1 (F1/G2/H1 boundaries) and J1 (H1/J2 boundaries) as prospective eyes. Neither was secured. The initial lower-right outline was nineteen potential points: E–J rows1–3 (15), E4/F4/G4 (3), F5 (1). Left18 plus19 would only draw before any contested upper-left gains. Black's E3/F3/G3/H3 quickly denied most of that outline.

F1 secured the western G1 boundary, but Black J2 denied the second corner boundary. The five White stones E2/F1/F2/G2/H2 ended with E1/G1/H1 only. E1 bordered connected Black D1; it was not an eye.

Manual final-board capture proofs:
- W H1, B E1 leaves six White stones G1/J1. W J1 captures nothing because Black J2 retains J3, leaving only G1; B G1 captures seven. W G1 instead leaves J1, where B J1 joins J2 and captures seven.
- W E1, B H1 leaves only G1. W G1 is suicide because Black H1 retains J1; B G1 captures six.
- W G1, B E1 leaves H1. W H1 adds only J1; B J1 joins J2 and captures seven.
- W J1 is isolated with only H1; B H1 captures it. The main group then has E1/G1, and White's fill at either lets Black capture at the other.
- W J3 is suicide on the final board: H3/J4/J2 are Black and none is captured.

These are manual branches, not official dead-stone adjudication. The five lower-right stones remained on the board at resignation. No numerical score was claimed.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k: four wins, nine losses, one draw. Two early footholds do not by themselves supply enough area or boundary turns.
2. Before EACH threat, list the new stone's empty orthogonal neighbors and the resulting connected group's liberties. J8 added none and left only H6.
3. Check the opponent's immediate capture before reading a response to atari. B H6 captured first and reopened the threatened Black groups' liberties.
4. Finish two eyes while multiple outside routes remain. F7/G6/H7 and a capture did not secure upper life; F8/H8/G9 denied the second space.
5. Rebuild after every capture. A7 reopened A6 and enabled an otherwise dead lower group to escape; A6/B7 then made real connections.
6. Preserve the exact A2/B1 shared-eye proof. A1 stayed isolated, but both same-color groups retained both eyes. Do not fill either to connect.
7. Count existing enemy stones out of geometric targets. F6 was Black before the upper estimate and had to be excluded. Keep secure18 separate from unsecured outlines and reductions.

# Game 17: Black vs 20k — B+8

Played 2026-10-05. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 86–87: 87 moves, 85 stone moves.
Final captures: Black 16, White 2. No invalid move or resignation.
The final scoring display matches the last playing board; no further dead-stone removal was needed.

The 20k record is now four wins, eight losses and one draw. Retain 20k. Both Black footholds lived, and sufficient area was counted before passing. Important territorial gains still depended on ignored ataris; this is not a forced opening win.

## Records and verified result

- game-017.sgf contains all 87 moves.
- game-017-log.json contains all 44 play responses, complete moves, returned-board group/liberty inventories, counting notes and the independent final count. Inventories for the first four responses were reconstructed after play; subsequent inventories were inspected during play.
- Official result and independent count agree: Black 48, White 33 plus 7 komi = 40, B+8.
- Black: 41 stones + 7 territory. White: 26 stones + 7 territory. No neutral points.
- Black area by rows 1–9: 9, 8, 6, 4, 6, 6, 4, 3, 2 = 48.
- White area by rows 1–9: 0, 1, 3, 5, 3, 3, 5, 6, 7 = 33.

- White territory: A8, B7, B9, C8, D7, D9, E8.

## Opening: three footholds, then actual lower connections

1 B C3, 2 W E5, 3 B G7, 4 W C7, 5 B G3, 6 W F4,
7 B E3, 8 W F3, 9 B F2, 10 W G4,
11 B G2, 12 W H3, 13 B E2, 14 W E4,
15 B D3, 16 W A4, 17 B B4, 18 W C6, 19 B C4, 20 W D5.

White F3 cut between E3/G3. F2 had real empty neighbors E2/F1/G2; G2 connected it to G3, E2 joined E3, and D3 joined C3. G3 had only G2/H3 after White G4, so the G2 connection mattered. C4 later joined B4 to the main lower group.

The move-10 note estimated only about 26 unsecured lower points. After move 14, the more explicit target was rows 1–2 all nine plus seven row-3 points excluding F3/H3 = 25. An upper-right F–J outline in rows 6–9 would add 16, totaling only 41. Neither group had eyes, and no secure area was claimed. This estimate correctly required more development, but depended on unprotected corner and upper boundaries.

B4/C4 contested additional lower-left space; the upper-right foothold had already been placed at move 3. This avoided relying entirely on a forty-point lower framework followed by a late unsupported invasion. The played replies do not establish that this opening is optimal.

## Upper life: preserve boundaries and connect the isolated edge stone

21 B F7, 22 W E7, 23 B G6, 24 W F8,
25 B G8, 26 W F6, 27 B G5, 28 W H4,
29 B H5, 30 W J4, 31 B J5, 32 W G9,
33 B H8, 34 W J8, 35 B H9, 36 W F9,
37 B J7, 38 W D8, 39 B H7, 40 W E9,
41 B J9 captured J8, 42 W J6, 43 B H6 captured J6.

G8 answered the F8 undercut; G5/H5/J5 secured the lower boundary before White descended farther. G9 challenged the upper boundary, but H8 then H9 prevented White's G9 and J8 stones from joining through H9. White F9 saved G9 by joining F8.

J7 put White J8 in atari at J9, but Black J7 itself was disconnected with exactly H7/J6. White D8 ignored that local fight. H7 promptly connected J7 through G7/H8; do not skip this connection when transplanting the idea.

After J9 captured J8, the two independent spaces were J8 and H6/J6. White J6 had only H6; H6 captured it and left true single-point eyes:
- J6: H6/J5/J7 boundaries.
- J8: H8/J7/J9 boundaries.
All boundaries were one connected Black group. Neither eye can be filled by White without suicide.

This supplied fifteen living area: upper rows 5–9 gave 3, 3, 4, 3, 2. The lower region still needed about thirty.

## Lower-left cleanup and life

44 W A3, 45 B B3, 46 W B1,
47 B C1, 48 W C2, 49 B D1, 50 W A5,
51 B D2, 52 W E1,
53 B B2 captured C2, 54 W A1,
55 B A2 captured A1/B1, 56 W A1,
57 B H2, 58 W C5.

White C2 put C1 in atari at D1. D1 saved it, and D2 then joined C1/D1 to the main group while putting C2 in atari at B2. White E1 ignored that atari and itself had only F1. B2 captured C2, securing true C2 with connected B2/C1/C3/D2 boundaries.

White A1 extended B1 to two stones with only A2. A2 captured both and connected directly through B2. White's repeated A1 entry had only B1. It was left enclosed while Black contested boundary points, then B1 captured it at move 85.

F1 at move 71 later captured E1 and secured true E1, bordered by D1/E2/F1. C2/E1 were already an explicit two-eye proof before final cleanup; A1 and A3/A4 provided additional eyes afterward. Lower life did not depend on a ko boundary.

## Two ignored ataris supplied the winning margin

59 B B5, 60 W B6,
61 B A6 captured A3/A4/A5, 62 W A7,
63 B A5 connected A6.

After B5, the three White left-edge stones had exactly A6. White B6 joined the central White group but ignored this atari. A6 captured three and gained A5/A7 as liberties. White A7 then left isolated Black A6 with only A5. Black A5 immediately connected it through B5; capturing alone was not enough. This preserved A3/A4 and added A5/A6 within the lower region.

64 W J2, 65 B F5, 66 W H1,
67 B E6 captured F6, 68 W D6,
69 B F6 connected E6, 70 W G1,
71 B F1 captured E1, 72 W J3.

F5 joined the living upper group and put isolated White F6 in atari at E6. White H1 ignored it. E6 captured F6, gaining D6/F6; White D6 then left isolated E6 only F6. F6 promptly joined it to F5/F7/G6. These three new area points—F5/E6/F6—expanded the upper living region from fifteen to eighteen.

White could have answered either atari rather than supplying these captures. The result validates the actual captures and connections, not an opening as forced against every reply.

## Right corner: read the recapture and then change the plan

73 B J1 captured G1/H1, 74 W H1 captured J1,
75 B D4, 76 W G1,
77 B J1 captured G1/H1, 78 W H1 captured J1,
79 B G1, 80 W B8,
81 B J1 captured H1, 82 W C9,
83 B H1 connected J1, 84 W A9,
85 B B1 captured A1, 86 W pass, 87 B pass.

The first two J1 captures each removed TWO White stones. Isolated Black J1 then had only H1. White H1 captured it and had G1/J1 as two liberties. These were legal recaptures, not ko: the preceding two White stones were not restored.

The inventory constrained the reading: do not count those captures as a secured right corner. D4 took an additional boundary point while White repeated G1. After the second exchange, G1 connected through F1/G2 and left White H1 only J1. White B8 ignored this atari.

The third J1 capture removed just ONE White stone. Here immediate White H1 would restore the preceding board, so simple ko would forbid it. This transient ko is inferred manually; the tool's returned position was after White C9 and showed ko none. No immediate recapture was attempted. H1 then connected J1 to G1/H2 and eliminated the vulnerable isolated boundary.

Before D4/G1 were resolved, the explicitly provisional outline was lower 28 + upper 18 = 46; losing both contested points would give 44, a draw. D4/G1 were secured, and the final H1/J1 gain added two, yielding 48. No arithmetic correction was needed in the final row count.

## Final life and carry forward

The final lower group had 25 stones and five territory points = 30; the upper group had 16 stones and two eyes = 18. No major Black group died. White captured only the two isolated J1 stones during the right-corner exchanges.

White's final stones were several disconnected groups, but each retained at least two separate shared eye liberties. The seven single-point White eyes had only White boundaries; an attempted Black fill captures none because every adjacent boundary group retains another liberty. Thus their disconnected appearance did not imply dead stones.

1. Retain 20k: four wins, eight losses, one draw. One win after a draw is not consistent strength.
2. Establish a second foothold while it has real room. Keep the explicit upper J6/J8 life proof and lower C2/E1 proof; do not generalize the opening as forced.
3. After every capture, inspect the new stone. A6 needed A5; E6 needed F6; J1 initially allowed a legal recapture.
4. Count contested points separately. D4/G1 mattered before passing; final 30 + 18 = 48 matched B+8.
5. Distinguish a two-stone capture from a one-stone ko. The J1/H1 exchanges changed character only after G1 became Black.
6. The three left captures and central F6 capture relied on ignored ataris. Preserve the tactical habits without claiming they will recur against stronger opponents.

All moves and variations were manual. Code only inspected current returned positions, counted groups/liberties/area, kept records and converted moves to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 11: Black vs 20k — B+2

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 58–59: 59 total moves, 56 stone moves and three passes (56, 58, 59).
Final captures: Black 1, White 0. No invalid move, ko, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

This is the first Black win and second consecutive win at 20k, following five losses there. Retain 20k to establish repeatability; neither the opening nor the corner rescue is proven best or forced.

## Records and verified score

- game-011.sgf contains all 59 moves.
- game-011-log.json contains opponent selection, all 30 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty and empty-region inventories, full move list, in-game counting notes and verified final area.
- Official result: Black wins by 2 points.
- Independent count: Black 29 stones + 16 territory = 45; White 26 stones + 10 territory = 36. White plus komi = 43. All 81 points assigned, no neutral area.
- Lower Black region: 19 stones + 14 empty points = 33.
- Upper-right Black region: nine connected stones + isolated J9 + two separate eyes = 12.
- Lower region by rows: row 1 all nine; row 2 all nine; row 3 A/B/C/F/G/H (six); row 4 A/B/C/G (four); row 5 A/B/C/D (four); row 6 B6 (one). Total 33.
- Upper region by rows: row 6 H6 (one); row 7 F/G/H/J (four); row 8 F/G/H/J (four); row 9 G/H/J (three). Total 12.
- Black territory: A1/A2/A3/A4/B1/B2/B3/B4/C1/D1/E1/F1, G2, J1, H9, J8.
- White territory: A8/A9/B8/B9/C8/C9/D7/D8/D9, F5.

## Opening and connections

1 B C3, 2 W E5, 3 B G7, 4 W C7,
5 B G3, 6 W E3, 7 B C5, 8 W G5,
9 B E2, 10 W F4, 11 B F3, 12 W H4,

E2 contested the lower side beneath White E3. F3 connected to G3; H3 blocked the right-side descent. - Game 1: Black vs 9d, Chinese area scoring, komi 7. Lost by resignation after White move 56 (D2).

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.

After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.
28. An extension into one temporary liberty is not an escape. In game 8, White E4 added F4, which Black immediately occupied. The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.

The final scoring board equals the last playing board; no additional dead-stone removal.

The 20k record is now four wins, ten losses and one draw. Retain 20k. The thirty-one surviving Black stones all joined one living group, and the six-stone left invasion was captured. The resulting framework still scored only 39. A six-point shift from White to Black would win; five would only draw at 44–37.

## Records and verified score

- game-019.sgf contains all 70 moves and RE[W+10].
- game-019-log.json contains all 35 play responses, each complete returned board and current-board group/liberty/empty-region inventory, full moves, decision notes, early outlines and final row count. Opponent selection is recorded as metadata, not as a raw selection response.
- Official and independent result agree: Black 39, White 42 plus 7 = 49, W+10.
- Black: 31 stones + eight territory. White: 24 stones + eighteen territory. No neutral points.
- Black area by rows 1–9: 1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 4, 4, 3, 6 = 39.
- White area by rows 1–9: 8, 6, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 3 = 42.
- Black territory: C4, E4 and A7/A8/A9/B5/B6/B7.
- All choices and hypothetical variations were manual. Code only inspected current positions, counted groups/liberties/area, kept records and converted moves to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation.

## Opening and early counts

1 B C3, 2 W G7, 3 B C7, 4 W G3,
5 B E5, 6 W G5, 7 B E3, 8 W E7,
9 B D7, 10 W E6, 11 B F5, 12 W F6,
13 B F4, 14 W G4, 15 B F3, 16 W D8.

Two early footholds did not mean two independent territorial bases: both C3 and C7 were on the left, while White owned both right corners. E5 contested the center, but Black's expansion still needed to produce enough area.

After move 10, explicitly unsecured outline A–D all rows (36) plus E1–E5 (5) = 41. F5/F4/F3 sought the needed additional five F-column points in rows 1–5, giving an unsecured target of 46 after Black F3. No eyes or secure territory were claimed. F3 actually joined E3 and F4; this was a real orthogonal connection, not a diagonal assumption.

White D8 contested D8/D9, reducing that rough target to 44. White F2 later removed F1/F2 prospects, and E1 removed another point. The lower F1/F2 region had been an unprotected outline, not established territory.

The strategic problem was identified early but not solved with a sufficient margin. Center expansion to F3–F5 added real boundary points; it did not prevent the undercuts. Earlier E1, earlier D2/D3 connection, or different opening/side development are hypotheses only. No single winning replacement was verified.

## Top expansion: preserve the actual connection route

17 B C8, 18 W F8, 19 B D6, 20 W F2,
21 B E2, 22 W G2, 23 B D9, 24 W E8,
25 B E9, 26 W E1, 27 B D1, 28 W F1,
29 B F9, 30 W G9, 31 B C9, 32 W H8,
33 B D5, 34 W D2.

C8 secured the upper-left boundary. D6 joined D7 and retained the D5 route to E5. E2 joined E3 and stopped F2 from descending directly to the left.

D9 had C9/E9 and ataried D8 at E8; White E8 connected its upper stones. E9 then had C9/F9 through D9. F9 had C9/G9 through D9/E9. After White G9, the three top stones were in atari with exactly C9. Black C9 immediately joined them to C8. D5 later joined the upper group through D6 to E5/F5.

The gained D9/E9/F9 points were real in the played sequence. They were safe because C9 remained available and was used promptly after atari, not because a one-line strip itself supplied eyes. Opponent alternatives were not exhaustively verified.

After move 28 the explicit potential count was A–D36 minus D8 one + E9 one + E2–E5 four + F3–F5 three = 43. F9 raised it to44, only a draw if all of it survived. The lower invasion subsequently removed five previously included points: B1/C1/D1/C2/D2. Capturing the later left invasion only restored the rest of that outline, yielding39.

## Lower mistake: an immediate atari rescue can still end in capture

White E1 at move26 had D1/F1. Black D1 at move27 had C1/D2 and put E1 in atari; White F1 simply joined E1 to F2/G2/G3/G4/G5. No capture was forced.

After White D2 at move34:
- Black D1 had only C1.
- White D2 had C2/D3.
- Black C3 was still disconnected from E3.

35 B C1, 36 W C2, 37 B D3, 38 W B1 captured C1/D1.

C1 added B1/C2, but White C2 immediately left C1/D1 only B1. Manual reading on that current board: B B1, W B2 leaves the three Black stones only A1; B A1 adds A2 but leaves four only A2; W A2 captures four. Merely extending the atari did not demonstrate a rescue.

Black D3 instead joined C3 to E3 and put C2/D2 in atari at B2 while accepting the two-stone loss. White B1 captured C1/D1 and reopened both points as liberties for C2/D2. The counter-atari was explicitly not treated as forcing. This limited the immediate sacrificed stones relative to the read extension, but it did not prove D3 globally optimal or forced.

The earlier mistake to review is creating the first-line D1 group without securing its D2 connection. Reconsider before D1, or before White D2. Earlier E1 or D2/D3 development are plausible candidates, not verified wins.

## Lower recovery and the changing A1 recapture

39 B B3, 40 W A3, 41 B A4, 42 W A2,
43 B B2, 44 W D1,
45 B A1 captured A2/A3, 46 W A2 captured A1,
47 B A3, 48 W pass,
49 B A1 captured A2, 50 W C1,
51 B A2, 52 W H6.

B3 connected to C3 and contained upward expansion. A4 had A5/B4 and ataried White A3 at A2; White A2 extended. B2 joined B3, left A2/A3 only A1, and White D1 instead joined C2/D2 to E1.

The first A1 capture removed TWO White stones. Black A1 then had only A2, because B1 remained White. White A2 legally recaptured Black A1 and retained A1/A3. This was not ko: recapture did not restore the two removed White stones.

Black A3 then joined A4 directly to B3 and put the new White A2 in atari at A1. White passed. The second A1 capture removed just ONE stone; Black A1 again had only A2, and immediate White A2 would now restore the preceding board. This transient simple ko is manually inferred; the tool returned after White C1 and showed ko none. No immediate recapture was attempted.

White C1 saved B1 by joining it to the large lower/right White group. Black A2 immediately connected isolated A1 through A3/B2, ending the vulnerability. The recovered corner did not restore B1/C1/D1/C2/D2.

## Explicit life before containing the left invasion

53 B D4, 54 W B6,
55 B C5, 56 W B5,
57 B B4, 58 W B7.

D4 secured true E4 with D4/E3/E5/F4 boundaries.
C5 then B4 secured true C4 with B4/C3/C5/D4 boundaries.
Every boundary belonged to the same connected Black group. Either attempted White fill would have no liberty and capture nothing because the other eye remained.

This life proof was complete at move57, before the invasion's later capture. Do not claim the capture alone supplied life.

59 B B8, 60 W A8, 61 B B9, 62 W A7,
63 B A5, 64 W A9, 65 B C6, 66 W J7,
67 B A6 captured six, 68 W H5.

B8 joined C8 and blocked the upper escape. B9 joined B8/C9 and secured the corner boundary. An earlier proposed Black A7 at the move61 position would have had only A6; White A6 could capture it and reopen A7. That false forcing counter-atari was rejected.

A5 joined A4 and denied the lower endpoint. After White A9, six White stones A7/A8/A9/B5/B6/B7 had exactly A6/C6. Black C6 directly joined C5/C7/D6 and left them only A6. White A6 would add no liberty, capture no Black boundary (Black retained C4/E4), and was suicide. Black A6 captured all six and connected directly through A5.

The six captured points became additional Black territory. This preserved a thirty-nine-point framework; it did not enlarge its border. The invasion failed because Black first secured life and then retained both outside edge boundaries.

## Final White life and completion

69 B pass, 70 W pass. W+10.

No supported additional gain was identified after the right framework closed. Black preserved C4/E4 and finished capturing the dead left stones before passing. This does not establish that every earlier right invasion would fail or that passing was globally optimal; it records the actual completion and the verified score.

White's disconnected appearance did not imply dead stones. The six-stone central group and G7 both retained F7/G8 as separate fully White-bordered eye points; all boundary groups adjacent to either retained another liberty. G9 retained G8/H9, H8 retained G8/H7/H9/J8, and J7 retained H7/J6/J8. The large lower/right White group had abundant enclosed right-side space. The final one-color empty-region count matched the official score without dead-stone removal.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k: four wins, ten losses, one draw. Secure life improved this game; sufficient area did not.
2. Act on the deficit earlier. An unsecured46 became44 before the lower capture, and the final39 requires a six-point shift to win. Same-side footholds can still amount to one insufficient framework.
3. Before placing a first-line stone, read the opponent's perpendicular cut and the eventual end of the atari extension. D1/C1 were lost after D2/C2; B1/A1 would only have added two more stones to the shown capture.
4. Keep the top connection habit: D9/E9/F9 retained C9, and C9 was played immediately when G9 left them in atari.
5. Rebuild every recapture. A1 first captured two and allowed W A2; later it captured one into transient ko. A2 then made the real connection.
6. Keep actual two-eye proof C4/E4 before containing invasions. B8/B9/A5/C6/A6 killed the left six while preserving both eyes; no imagined ko or seki was needed.
